blocks.content: Every request that reaches your application, whether it is an HTTP call, a Lambda invocation, or a message off a queue, needs a place to land first. This lesson looks at how that landing spot should relate to the code that actually does the work behind it.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters

When an app is small, it is tempting to put everything inside the one function that handles a request: parse the input, check the rules, hit the database, and format a response, all in the same place. That works fine for a weekend project.

It stops working the moment that same logic needs to run somewhere else too, a background job, a CLI script, a second endpoint, or a unit test that has no business starting a web server. Untangling the business logic from the code that receives the request is exactly the problem a controller and a service split solves.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889900280-587460460.png
blocks.alt: Hotel receptionist relaying a check in request to the back office instead of doing the work herself

blocks.content: Think about walking up to a hotel front desk and saying I would like to check in. The receptionist does not personally go clean a room, look up which rooms are free, or manage the housekeeping schedule. Behind the counter, a back office handles inventory and housekeeping. The receptionist just takes your request, waits for the real work to happen, and hands you back a key and a room number.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889902163-910999685.png
blocks.alt: Call center agent forwarding an account change to a specialized back office team

blocks.content: A customer service call is built the same way. The agent who picks up your call cannot personally change your account balance or update your billing address on the spot. They note down what you need, pass it to a specialized back office team authorized to make the actual change, then relay the confirmation back to you once it is done. The agent is the controller, the back office team is the service.
3. Problem It Solves & Definition
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889903620-651350480.png
blocks.alt: A fat handler mixing routing and business logic compared to a thin controller delegating to a service

blocks.content: As soon as an application grows past a toy example, a single function that reads the request, checks business rules, talks to the database, and formats the response becomes impossible to reuse or test in isolation. You cannot call the pricing logic from a scheduled job without dragging along parsing code that has nothing to do with pricing.

The fix is to draw a firm line between the code that receives a request and the code that decides what to do about it. Everything on the receiving side becomes a controller or handler, everything that makes decisions and touches data becomes a service, and the controller only ever calls into the service, never the other way around.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: A controller, or handler, is the entry point that accepts an incoming request, handles routing and transport level concerns, and immediately delegates to a service. A service is the class that owns the actual business logic, the calculations, validations and rules the controller has no opinion about.
4. Key Terminology

["Controller: the entry point that receives an incoming request and decides which service to call, without performing the business logic itself.","Handler: the term many frameworks use in place of controller, such as an AWS Lambda handler or an Express route handler, functionally the same role.","Service: the class that holds the actual business logic, the rules, calculations and decisions the application exists to make.","Delegation: the act of a controller handing off work to a service instead of performing that work inline.","Thin controller: a controller that only parses the request, validates its shape, and delegates, considered the healthy default.","Fat controller: an anti pattern where business logic leaks into the controller, making it hard to test and reuse."]
items: Controller: the entry point that receives an incoming request and decides which service to call, without performing the business logic itself.
Handler: the term many frameworks use in place of controller, such as an AWS Lambda handler or an Express route handler, functionally the same role.
Service: the class that holds the actual business logic, the rules, calculations and decisions the application exists to make.
Delegation: the act of a controller handing off work to a service instead of performing that work inline.
Thin controller: a controller that only parses the request, validates its shape, and delegates, considered the healthy default.
Fat controller: an anti pattern where business logic leaks into the controller, making it hard to test and reuse.

blocks.content: 5. Visual Diagram
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889905173-764961070.png
blocks.alt: A request flowing from client through controller to service to repository and back

blocks.content: Every request flows in the same direction: in through the controller, straight to the service, out through whatever data layer the service depends on. The result then flows back along the exact same path in reverse. The controller only ever talks to the service, it never reaches past it into the database or any other layer directly.
6. Syntax & Code Example

The shape is always the same regardless of language or framework: a controller method receives a request, immediately calls exactly one service method, and returns whatever that method gives back. Nothing resembling a business rule appears inside the controller body.

Now apply that same shape to something closer to a real application. OrderController.placeOrder receives the request and delegates immediately to OrderService.processOrder, which is where stock is checked and the total is actually calculated:
7. Code Breakdown

["OrderController.placeOrder(request): receives the request and does nothing but forward it to orderService.processOrder(request), the entire method body is one line of delegation.","Stock check loop: OrderService walks every item against stockByProduct before touching anything else, so an order with insufficient stock fails fast with no side effects.","Total calculation: sums quantity times unitPrice across every item, this is the actual business rule for pricing an order.","Stock deduction: only runs after both the stock check and the total calculation succeed, so a rejected order never mutates any state.","OrderResult: a plain data object that flows from the service back through the controller and out to the caller, it carries no framework specific baggage at all."]
items: OrderController.placeOrder(request): receives the request and does nothing but forward it to orderService.processOrder(request), the entire method body is one line of delegation.
Stock check loop: OrderService walks every item against stockByProduct before touching anything else, so an order with insufficient stock fails fast with no side effects.
Total calculation: sums quantity times unitPrice across every item, this is the actual business rule for pricing an order.
Stock deduction: only runs after both the stock check and the total calculation succeed, so a rejected order never mutates any state.
OrderResult: a plain data object that flows from the service back through the controller and out to the caller, it carries no framework specific baggage at all.

9. Behind the Scenes (Routing and Dependency Injection)
blocks.text: 9. Behind the Scenes (Routing and Dependency Injection)

blocks.content: 9.1 How a Router Finds Your Handler
blocks.text: 9.1 How a Router Finds Your Handler

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889909757-733903313.png
blocks.alt: A router matching an incoming URL and method to a registered handler method

blocks.content: Frameworks maintain a routing table that maps an incoming URL and HTTP method to exactly one handler function. When a request for a path like POST orders arrives, the router looks up that combination, finds the function registered as OrderController.placeOrder, and invokes it directly. This lookup step is exactly why the entry point is often literally called a handler.
9.2 How the Service Gets Wired Into the Controller
blocks.text: 9.2 How the Service Gets Wired Into the Controller

blocks.content: The controller does not usually build its own service with new. A dependency injection container constructs the service once, then hands, or injects, that ready made instance into every controller that asks for it. This is why controllers so often receive their service through a constructor parameter instead of creating one manually, the framework wires the two layers together and keeps the controller decoupled from how the service itself gets built.
10. Real-World Use Cases & Industry Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889912060-432821703.png
blocks.alt: The controller service split applied across e-commerce, banking, social media and gaming request flows

blocks.content: ["E-commerce: an OrderController receives a checkout request and delegates to an OrderService for stock checks and pricing, exactly like the worked example above.","Banking: a TransferController accepts a transfer request and hands it to a TransferService, which enforces balance checks and ledger rules.","Social Media: a PostController takes a new post request and delegates moderation, feed distribution, and storage to a PostService.","Gaming: a MatchController receives a join request and delegates the actual matchmaking rules to a MatchService."]
items: E-commerce: an OrderController receives a checkout request and delegates to an OrderService for stock checks and pricing, exactly like the worked example above.
Banking: a TransferController accepts a transfer request and hands it to a TransferService, which enforces balance checks and ledger rules.
Social Media: a PostController takes a new post request and delegates moderation, feed distribution, and storage to a PostService.
Gaming: a MatchController receives a join request and delegates the actual matchmaking rules to a MatchService.

blocks.content: This split is not a theoretical ideal, it is baked directly into the most widely used frameworks in the industry.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784889914494-726869873.png
blocks.alt: A Spring MVC RestController annotated class delegating to a Service annotated class which uses a Repository bean

blocks.content: In Spring MVC, a class annotated @RestController handles the HTTP request, binds the incoming JSON into a request object, and calls straight into a class annotated @Service, which is where the actual business logic and repository calls live. AWS Lambda follows the identical shape at a smaller scale: the handler function receives the event and immediately calls out to a service class that does the real work, the handler itself stays a thin, replaceable adapter.
11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["Business logic can be unit tested directly against the service, with no HTTP framework involved at all.","Introduces an extra layer and an extra class for even the simplest operations."],["The same service can be called from a REST controller, a message queue consumer, or a scheduled job without duplicating logic.","An overly thin controller can turn into pointless pass through boilerplate if the service is never reused anywhere else."],["Swapping frameworks, such as moving a handler from Express to a Lambda function, only touches the controller layer, not the business rules.","Without discipline, business logic quietly creeps back into the controller and the separation stops being real."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Putting validation, calculations, or database calls directly inside the controller method instead of the service.","Letting the controller construct its own service with new instead of receiving it through dependency injection, which makes testing much harder.","Returning framework specific objects straight out of the service, coupling business logic to a transport layer it should know nothing about.","Creating a service that does nothing but wrap a single repository call, which just moves the fat controller problem into a fat, meaningless service."]
items: Putting validation, calculations, or database calls directly inside the controller method instead of the service.
Letting the controller construct its own service with new instead of receiving it through dependency injection, which makes testing much harder.
Returning framework specific objects straight out of the service, coupling business logic to a transport layer it should know nothing about.
Creating a service that does nothing but wrap a single repository call, which just moves the fat controller problem into a fat, meaningless service.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Keep the controller method to a handful of lines: parse the request, call one service method, shape the response.","Let the service accept and return plain data objects, never framework specific request or response types.","Inject the service through the constructor so tests can substitute a fake or mock version without touching the controller at all.","Name methods on the service after the business action they perform, like processOrder, not after the HTTP verb that happened to trigger them."]
items: Keep the controller method to a handful of lines: parse the request, call one service method, shape the response.
Let the service accept and return plain data objects, never framework specific request or response types.
Inject the service through the constructor so tests can substitute a fake or mock version without touching the controller at all.
Name methods on the service after the business action they perform, like processOrder, not after the HTTP verb that happened to trigger them.

blocks.content: 13. Key Takeaways & Cheat Sheet

["A controller, or handler, is the entry point that receives a request and handles transport level concerns like routing and status codes.","A service holds the actual business logic and gets called by the controller, never the other way around.","Handler and controller describe the same role, different frameworks such as AWS Lambda, Express, and Spring just prefer different names for it.","A thin controller that only delegates is the goal, business logic creeping into it is the anti pattern to watch for.","Dependency injection is what lets a controller receive a ready made service instance instead of constructing one itself."]
items: A controller, or handler, is the entry point that receives a request and handles transport level concerns like routing and status codes.
A service holds the actual business logic and gets called by the controller, never the other way around.
Handler and controller describe the same role, different frameworks such as AWS Lambda, Express, and Spring just prefer different names for it.
A thin controller that only delegates is the goal, business logic creeping into it is the anti pattern to watch for.
Dependency injection is what lets a controller receive a ready made service instance instead of constructing one itself.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked to explain the difference between a controller and a service, lead with the direction of the call: the controller calls the service, and the service never calls back into the controller or knows anything about HTTP. That one sentence covers the entire responsibility split.
